Free tools

Claude Code Hooks Security Check

Paste a Claude Code hooks configuration and see which hook command strings match a known-dangerous shape — a remote download piped straight into a shell, a credential file read and sent over the network in the same line, an unguarded recursive delete, TLS verification disabled, and more. Hooks run automatically, with no confirmation prompt, on every matching tool call.

Textual pattern checks, not a safety guarantee. This tool never runs your commands and never calls an LLM — it only matches the text you paste against known-dangerous shapes. A match is worth a look, not a verdict, and a clean scan is not proof a command is safe. See why a clean scan isn't a safety guarantee.

1. Paste your hooks configuration

Either a full settings.json (its "hooks" key is used) or a standalone hooks object like {"PreToolUse": [...]}. Nothing here is uploaded — everything runs in this page.

Findings

0high-severity
0medium-severity
0caution

Paste a hooks configuration above, or load the example, then press Scan.

    Usage is optional, stays in this browser, and counts only that a scan ran or a summary was copied. Nothing you paste — no hook commands, paths, or findings — is ever recorded, uploaded, or sent to an analytics service. Uncheck to turn it off. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable counting automatically.

    Common questions

    What does this tool check in a hooks configuration?

    The command string inside every hook entry, against known-dangerous shapes: a remote download (curl/wget) piped straight into a shell interpreter, a PowerShell download executed with Invoke-Expression, an unguarded recursive delete of a broad path like / or $HOME, a credential file (SSH key, AWS credentials, .npmrc, kube config, and similar) read and sent over the network in the same line, environment variables dumped and sent over the network, TLS/certificate verification disabled, a shell startup file or crontab appended to, world-writable permissions granted, a base64-encoded payload decoded and executed, and a process started detached from the hook invocation.

    How is this different from Claude Code Settings Check?

    Claude Code Settings Check asks whether a hook or permission rule is shaped correctly -- does the matcher compile, is there a command at all. This tool assumes the JSON is well-formed and asks a different question: does the command text itself match a known-dangerous shape. Run both -- a hook can be structurally perfect and still risky, or structurally broken and harmless.

    Does this tool contact a network or execute my commands?

    No. Every check is a deterministic, textual pattern match against the command strings you paste, entirely in your browser. It never runs a single command and never uploads anything.

    Does a clean scan mean my hooks are safe?

    No. A zero-finding result means none of this tool's known patterns matched the text you pasted -- it does not mean a command is safe. A command can be dangerous in a way this tool doesn't recognise, and a command can match a pattern here and be completely ordinary (rm -rf on a build directory shares a shape with rm -rf on your home directory). See “Why a clean scan isn’t a safety guarantee” for what this tool can and can't see.

    Read why a clean scan isn't a safety guarantee, or see this checker vs. reading the hooks config by eye for what a manual read reliably catches and what it doesn't.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not security advice, and it is not a guarantee that a command is safe or unsafe. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for reviewing every hook command yourself regardless of what this tool reports. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

    Privacy. Everything runs client-side in your browser. The configuration you paste, and every finding this tool produces, never leaves your device — there is no upload, no server-side processing, and no third-party analytics vendor.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record.

    Checking whether a hook or permission rule is shaped correctly instead? See Claude Code Settings Check. Auditing an MCP server's launch config instead? See MCP Config Risk Check. Checking a Claude Code subagent definition instead? See Claude Code Subagent Check. Checking a Claude Code Skill's frontmatter instead? See Skill Manifest Check.

vs-reading-the-hooks-config-by-eye.html.text:
← Claude Code Hooks Security Check

Claude Code Hooks Security Check vs. reading the hooks config by eye

Reading a short hooks config with one obvious curl-to-shell download catches that download. It reliably misses a credential read and network send split across a pipe, an environment dump piped to curl, a base64-decoded payload piped to a shell, and a broad rm -rf buried inside a longer chain of statements — which is what this free, no-upload checker computes exactly, in one pass.

Where reading it yourself stops being enough

Anyone about to trust a hooks configuration already does this: open settings.json, read each hook's command string, and decide whether it looks right before letting it fire automatically and unattended. For a single hook with an obviously broad curl | bash, that read catches it. The problem is the other ten checks below are not the kind of thing a skim of a rendered command string reliably surfaces, especially once a config carries several hooks across several events.

What you're trying to confirmReading the config yourselfThis checker
A command pipes a curl/wget download straight into a shell interpreter, or downloads with PowerShell and executes it with Invoke-Expression.Works. This is the one case a plain read reliably catches.Also catches it, in the same pass as everything below.
A command reads a credential path (SSH key, AWS credentials, .npmrc, kube config, and similar) and separately sends data out over the network, anywhere in the same command line.Easy to miss when the read and the send sit on opposite ends of a long piped or chained command with ordinary-looking steps between them.Matched as a pair — a sensitive path plus a network-send shape — in the same command, regardless of where each half sits.
Environment variables dumped (env/printenv/export -p) and piped or sent to a network command in the same line.The dump and the send can be several tokens apart in a chained command; easy to read each half as unremarkable on its own.Checked as a pair against the same command line, every time.
An unguarded recursive delete (rm -rf or equivalent flags) targeting a broad path like /, ~, or $HOME, possibly third or fourth in a &&/;-separated chain.Easy to skim past while reading left to right for the command's obvious purpose.Every statement in the chain split and checked for the same broad-delete shape.
TLS/certificate verification disabled on a request (curl -k, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0, and similar), which can sit as one flag among many.A single flag buried in a long argument list is easy to read past.Matched against the exact flag/variable shapes across every command, every time.
A base64-decoded payload piped straight into a shell — the dangerous part is hidden inside an encoded blob, not written as a readable command.Reads as an unremarkable-looking pipe unless you already know to treat decode-then-execute as the same risk as a plain download-to-shell.Flags the decode-then-execute pipe shape itself, with no need to decode or run anything.
Persistence via a shell startup file, crontab, or user service, so the command runs again later independent of this hook firing again.Requires noticing an append (>>) to a dotfile or a crontab/systemctl --user call buried in a longer line.Matched against the specific persistence-target shapes, every time.
World-writable permissions granted (chmod 777/a+w/o+w) and a process started detached from the hook (nohup/setsid/tmux -d and similar).Each is a short, easy-to-miss flag in a longer argument list.Checked against the exact flag shapes, across every command in the config.
Re-checking an entire hooks config again after adding or editing one hook.One hook at a time, remembered by hand, every time something changes.One paste, every command, every time.

A quick read is still the fastest way to catch an obviously dangerous command in a short config, and this checker is not doing anything a careful line-by-line audit couldn't — it is reading the same command strings a careful audit would, just checking every one against eleven fixed shapes automatically instead of leaving the comparison to be remembered by hand across however many hooks the config has.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: the browser page parses JSON you paste entirely in your own browser. It never sends your hooks configuration anywhere.

Common questions

Can't I just read the hooks config myself?

For a short config with one hook and an obvious curl-piped-to-bash download, yes -- that case is visible on a single read. What reading does not reliably catch is a credential file read and a network send that live in different parts of the same command line, an environment-variable dump piped to curl, a base64-decoded payload piped to a shell, or a broad rm -rf buried inside a longer chain of && and ; separated statements. Those need the whole command line checked against eleven separate shapes the same mechanical way every time, not remembered while skimming a settings.json with a dozen hooks in it.

Why is credential exfiltration easy to miss on a read-through?

Because the read of a sensitive path like ~/.ssh/id_rsa or ~/.aws/credentials and the curl -d or scp that sends it out can sit on opposite ends of a long piped or chained command, with ordinary-looking steps in between. A reviewer's eye catches either half in isolation easily; confirming both halves are present in the same command line, for every command in the config, is the kind of pairing a mechanical check does the same way every time and a skim does not.

Why is a base64-decoded payload piped to a shell hard to spot?

Because the dangerous part -- what actually runs -- is hidden inside an encoded blob, not written out as a readable command. The visible text is just "base64 -d | bash" or similar, which looks unremarkable next to a curl-to-shell download unless you already know to treat any decode-then-execute pipe as the same risk shape. This tool flags the pipe shape itself, without needing to decode or run the payload.

What about a broad rm -rf buried in a longer command?

A hook command chained with && or ; can run several statements in sequence, and an unguarded rm -rf ~ or rm -rf $HOME sitting third or fourth in that chain is easy to skim past while reading left to right for the command's obvious purpose. Splitting every command on its statement separators and checking each part for a broad, unguarded recursive delete is a mechanical pass through every clause, not a read of the parts that look load-bearing.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual habit anyone reviewing a Claude Code hooks configuration already has -- reading each hook's command text by eye before trusting it to fire unattended. It names no competing product or company. The checker itself makes no network request of any kind: the browser page parses pasted JSON in your own browser, and nothing you paste is ever uploaded.

Want to know what a zero-finding scan actually means? Read why a clean scan isn't a safety guarantee.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not a security audit, and it does not replace reviewing your own hooks configuration before trusting it to fire unattended. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

why-a-clean-scan-isnt-a-safety-guarantee.text:
← Claude Code Hooks Security Check

Why a clean scan isn't a safety guarantee

Zero findings means none of this tool's known-dangerous patterns matched the command text you pasted — not that the hooks you're about to trust are safe. Here is what a textual pattern scan can and can't see, and why the difference matters.

What "textual pattern" means here

Every check this tool runs looks for a specific, documented shape in a hook's command string: a download piped straight into a shell, a credential file read and sent over the network in the same line, environment variables dumped and sent over the network, an unguarded recursive delete, TLS verification disabled, persistence via a shell startup file or crontab, world-writable permissions, a base64-obfuscated payload executed, and a process started detached from the hook. These are common, well-known dangerous shapes — mechanized so they don't get missed on a rushed review of a hooks config someone else wrote.

What it can't see

Anything that isn't one of the specific shapes above, and anything hidden from a simple text match: a command built at runtime from a variable this tool can't see the value of, a shape phrased in a way the patterns don't recognise, a malicious MCP tool or script the command merely invokes by name without any of it appearing in the command string itself, or a legitimate-looking command whose actual danger only shows up given the environment it runs in. This tool never executes the command in a sandbox and observes what it does — it only reads the text.

This is the same reason a linter passing doesn't mean a test suite would: they check different, complementary things.

A match isn't always dangerous, either

Several patterns here are shapes shared by ordinary, safe commands. rm -rf on a build directory has the exact same shape as rm -rf on a home directory; nohup behind a legitimate long-running dev-server hook looks the same as one used to persist something unwanted. Every finding is worded as worth a look, not a verdict — reviewing the actual command in its real context is still yours to do.

What a clean scan is worth, then

It rules out the specific, common dangerous shapes above, cheaply, before you trust a hooks configuration someone else wrote or a project you just cloned — worth running on every hooks config before you let it fire unattended. Treat it as a floor: pair it with actually reading the commands, not a substitute for reading them.

Common questions

If a hooks scan comes back with zero findings, are my hooks safe?

No. A zero-finding result means none of this tool's known-dangerous patterns matched the command text you pasted -- it does not mean the hooks are safe to run unattended. The scan looks for specific textual shapes (a download piped into a shell, a credential read sent over the network, and the others it documents), not at what a command actually does when it runs, and it cannot see a shape it doesn't yet know about.

What can a textual pattern scan actually catch?

Command strings that match a documented, specific shape: a remote download piped straight into a shell interpreter, a credential file read and sent over the network in the same line, environment variables dumped and sent over the network, an unguarded recursive delete of a broad path, TLS verification disabled, persistence via a shell startup file or crontab, world-writable permissions, a base64-obfuscated payload executed, and a process started detached from the hook. These are common, well-known dangerous shapes -- mechanized so a rushed review doesn't miss one.

What can't it catch?

Anything that isn't one of the specific shapes above, and anything hidden from a simple text match: a command built at runtime from a variable this tool can't see the value of, a shape phrased in a way the patterns don't recognise, a malicious MCP tool or script the command merely invokes by name, or a legitimate-looking command whose actual danger only shows up given the environment it runs in. A textual scan cannot execute the command in a sandbox and observe what it does, and it does not try to.

Does a match always mean a command is dangerous?

No. Several patterns here are shapes shared by ordinary, safe commands -- rm -rf on a build directory has the same shape as rm -rf on a home directory; nohup for a legitimate long-running dev-server hook looks the same as one used to persist something unwanted. Every finding is worded as worth a look, not a verdict, and reviewing the actual command in context is still yours to do.

So what is a clean scan actually worth?

It rules out the specific, common dangerous shapes it checks for, cheaply, before you trust a hooks configuration someone else wrote or a project you just cloned -- the same value a linter has before a human review. Treat it as a floor: worth running on every hooks config you're about to trust, and worth pairing with actually reading the commands, not a substitute for reading them.
